countries.name: Mexico
countries.note: Mexico has experienced significant militarization since 2006's Calderón drug war deployment. Under AMLO and now Sheinbaum, the armed forces control the National Guard, oversee infrastructure megaprojects (Tren Maya, Felipe Ángeles Airport), and run the customs agency. This expansion of military economic roles raises structural concerns for democratic civilian control and civil-military theory.
countries.watch: CJNG leader El Mencho killed Feb 22 by SEDENA with US intelligence; 12 US Green Berets authorized at Mexican bases Feb 27. Monitor CJNG successor dynamics and whether Sheinbaum's deepened US military cooperation becomes institutionalized — or triggers backlash from sovereignty-focused sectors of the officer corps.

in_depth.subtitle: SEDENA Militarization · Cartel Wars · FTO Designations
in_depth.brief: Mexico presents the region's most complex civil-military case: deep structural militarization under a formally democratic civilian government that has not experienced a coup. The officer corps has not asserted political preferences but has been the consistent beneficiary of institutional expansion. The Sheinbaum administration has deepened the AMLO-era model: in July 2025, SEDENA was formally granted national security intelligence authority, and the National Guard was transferred to SEDENA command.

milestones.title: AMLO creates National Guard — civilian name, military personnel
milestones.desc: Constitutionally civilian in name only. Built from military cadre. Marks start of institutional re-militarization under new labels.

milestones.title: National Guard formally transferred to SEDENA
milestones.desc: Military takes AIFA airport, Tren Maya, ports, customs. Mexico has no nationwide civilian police force.

milestones.title: Sheinbaum takes office — deepens AMLO militarization model
milestones.desc: New SEDENA / SEMAR chiefs appointed Sep 2024. Maintains and expands military institutional roles.

milestones.title: Sinaloa civil war begins — El Mayo transferred to US
milestones.desc: Chapitos faction hands Zambada to US. Cartel splits: La Mayiza vs Chapitos. 2,197 homicides in Sinaloa state.

milestones.title: Trump designates 6 Mexican cartels as FTOs
milestones.desc: Sovereignty crisis. Sheinbaum deploys 10K NG to border to preempt tariffs. DEA access restricted.

milestones.title: SEDENA granted national security intelligence authority
milestones.desc: Legislative reform. Military now authorized to generate and act on national security intelligence without civilian co-lead.

milestones.title: El Mencho (CJNG) killed in joint SEDENA/SEMAR operation
milestones.desc: US JITC-CC intelligence and planning support. 25 National Guard members killed. Largest cartel takedown in years.

countries.name: Belize
countries.branches: Belize Defence Force (BDF) · Belize Police Department
countries.note: Belize has stable civil-military relations under a parliamentary system; John Briceño's PUP was re-elected in March 2025 with 26 of 31 seats. The BDF is small (~1,500 personnel) and focuses on the Guatemala border; the territorial dispute has been before the ICJ since 2019, with no active armed friction. In July 2026 the defence minister took leave during an audit of the ministry (2019–2026) following a procurement-payments scandal, and the PM assumed the portfolio. Narco-trafficking through the coastline and cays is the primary security challenge.
countries.watch: Guatemala-Belize ICJ process is the primary strategic risk; watch for any escalation in territorial friction. BDF capacity-building and US SOUTHCOM engagement are the key CMR variables.

countries.name: Costa Rica
countries.branches: Public Force (police) — no military by constitution
countries.note: Costa Rica abolished its military in 1948 (Article 12, Constitution), and the Public Force and border police perform all security functions. Organized-crime violence and cartel expansion are straining the civilian police model. Laura Fernández, Rodrigo Chaves's continuity successor, took office on May 8, 2026 on a 'mano dura' platform, with a megaprison and a police surveillance centre as early priorities. Pressure for militarized border and penal policy is rising, though no constitutional change has occurred.
countries.watch: Fernández's 'mano dura' agenda: monitor whether megaprison, surveillance, and border measures erode Costa Rica's constitutionally unarmed tradition, and whether Chaves's continuing role concentrates security policy in the executive.

officials.title: Minister of Public Security
officials.name: Gerald Campos Valverde
officials.note: No military; the security minister oversees the Public Force.

countries.name: El Salvador
countries.branches: Army · Navy · Air Force · National Police
countries.note: El Salvador under Nayib Bukele represents a significant democratic backsliding case. Following the 2021 Legislative Assembly takeover by Bukele's party, the Supreme Court was packed and constitutional term limits removed. Bukele has explicitly used the military as a personal political instrument, most notoriously in the February 2020 Legislative Assembly incident. The estado de excepción anti-gang crackdown (March 2022–present) has created mass detention conditions with minimal due process.
countries.watch: Estado de excepción hit 4 years March 27 (49th extension); 91,650+ detained, 504 deaths in custody, FAES military role in policing extended through Dec 2026. Watch for any judicial or international accountability mechanism and whether the US-Bukele alignment survives any shift in Washington's CECOT posture.

election.note: Bukele re-elected Feb 2024; second term through 2030

in_depth.subtitle: Régimen de Excepción · Civil-Military Fusion · CECOT
in_depth.brief: El Salvador represents a textbook case of democratic backsliding through civil-military fusion. Unlike classical coups, Bukele's consolidation proceeds via managed elections — enabled by judicial packing that reversed constitutional term limits — while using the military as a visible loyalty instrument and domestic enforcement mechanism. The February 2020 Legislative Assembly occupation was the defining inflection point.

milestones.title: Bukele inaugurated — begins military-adjacent posture
milestones.desc: Cabinet includes former military figures. Security policy emphasizes visibility of armed forces.

milestones.title: Bukele enters Assembly with armed soldiers — loyalty oath
milestones.desc: Officers publicly pledge loyalty to president. Constitutional crisis: military refuses to enforce legislative limits on executive.

milestones.title: Bukele-controlled Assembly removes Supreme Court magistrates
milestones.desc: Judicial packing removes institutional check. Plan announced to double army from 20K to 40K by 2026.

milestones.title: Régimen de Excepción declared — mass arrest campaign
milestones.desc: Following 80-homicide weekend. Military and police begin mass arrests. Suspension of due process rights.

milestones.title: CECOT mega-prison opens — military operates security
milestones.desc: Designed for 40,000 detainees. Military handles transport and perimeter. Military discipline applied to civilians.

milestones.title: Bukele re-elected with 85% — second term begins June 2024
milestones.desc: Despite constitutional ban on consecutive terms, reversed by packed court. No major military dissent recorded.

milestones.desc: US pays $6M/year. Deportees later report systematic torture per HRW report (Nov 2025).

milestones.title: Military deployed to disperse peaceful protests
milestones.desc: First post-civil war use of armed forces against civil society. Heinrich Böll Stiftung documents cases.

milestones.title: Constitutional reform: indefinite re-election, 6-year terms
milestones.desc: Assembly approves 57–3: abolishes runoffs, moves elections to 2027. Constitutional order restructured.

milestones.title: GIPES presents to CIDH: 504 in-custody deaths under régimen
milestones.desc: Findings of crimes against humanity submitted to Inter-American Commission. 48th régimen extension.

countries.name: Guatemala
countries.note: Guatemala's military retains significant political influence, particularly via its intelligence apparatus and historical impunity for genocide-era crimes. President Arévalo, a democracy reformist, faced an extraordinary political-legal siege before and after his 2023 election, with actors tied to the military-prosecutor nexus. His government's survival and consolidation of civilian control is the central CMR story in Guatemala.
countries.watch: Arévalo's ability to subordinate military intelligence to civilian oversight — specifically the Directorate of Military Intelligence (DIM) — is the structural test of his government.

countries.name: Honduras
countries.branches: Army · Navy · Air Force · National Police
countries.note: Honduras has historically shown high military institutional autonomy, rooted in its role as a U.S. Cold War platform and the 2009 coup. Ex-president Hernández (2014–2022), from the same National Party as the new government, was convicted in the U.S. of drug trafficking in 2024 and pardoned by President Trump in December 2025. Nasry Asfura took office on January 27, 2026. He named a corporate lawyer from his inner circle as defence secretary and pledged to strengthen the armed forces. The military's constitutional mandate for internal security functions as a structural prerogative, and the direction of anti-gang militarization under Asfura is the key variable.
countries.watch: The Asfura government (since Jan 2026): watch whether the Castro-era state of exception and military role in anti-gang and prison operations deepen, Joint Chiefs relations with the new civilian defence secretary, and US security cooperation (Soto Cano/JTF-Bravo).

countries.name: Nicaragua
countries.note: Nicaragua under Ortega has constructed an authoritarian civil-military system modeled loosely on Cuba and Venezuela. A February 2025 constitutional reform made Rosario Murillo co-president, extended terms to six years, and placed the army and police formally under the presidency. In July 2026 Ortega declared that Nicaragua 'will not have elections again.' The Army (EPS) is institutionally subordinate to the party rather than to civilian constitutional oversight. The 2018 suppression of the April uprising, in which over 300 were killed, involved coordinated military, police, and paramilitaries.
countries.watch: Ortega declared in Jul 2026 that there will be no more elections. Monitor succession dynamics under the Ortega–Murillo co-presidency, the loyalty of the EPS high command to Murillo, and emigration and economic stress.

election.note: Terms extended to six years in 2025; on Jul 19, 2026 Ortega said there will be no more elections.

countries.name: Panama
countries.branches: National Security Forces — no standing army
countries.note: Panama abolished its military following the 1989 US intervention (Just Cause). Security functions are performed by civilian National Security Forces. Panama's core security challenge is the Darién Gap — a major migration and narco-trafficking corridor — which has driven increasing securitization of the border zone. President Mulino, a former security minister, has taken a hardline border management approach with US support. Canal sovereignty remains the primary strategic concern and a source of US-Panama security tension under Trump.
countries.watch: Darién Gap narco-migration crisis is securitizing the border zone absent a formal army; monitor civilian force capacity and US SOUTHCOM engagement under canal sovereignty tensions with Trump administration.

countries.name: Cuba
countries.branches: FAR: Army · Navy · Air Defense · MTT
countries.note: Cuba's Revolutionary Armed Forces (FAR) are the institutional backbone of the Cuban state, owning a major share of the economy through GAESA holding group (tourism, retail, remittances). The civil-military boundary is structurally fused — the party, state, and military are not meaningfully distinct at the senior command level. Post-Castro succession dynamics are a key CMR watch item.
countries.watch: Economic collapse and unprecedented 2021–2024 emigration are straining FAR institutional capacity — monitor for any public expressions of dissent within the officer corps.

election.note: Non-competitive; FAR institutional continuity the key variable

countries.name: Dominican Republic
countries.branches: Army · Navy · Air Force · National Police
countries.note: The Dominican Republic maintains one of the more stable civil-military relationships in the Caribbean. President Abinader (re-elected May 2024 with 57%) maintains a cooperative military posture focused on Haiti border security and counter-narcotics. The military's role in constructing a border wall and managing migrant flows has expanded its domestic infrastructure mission without triggering institutional autonomy concerns. No significant civilian control challenges.
countries.watch: Haiti border management and military role in wall construction — monitor whether the security-driven expansion of military domestic roles sets precedents for institutional autonomy beyond the current civilian oversight framework.

election.note: Abinader re-elected with 57%; next presidential election 2028

countries.name: Guyana
countries.branches: Guyana Defence Force (GDF) · Guyana Police Force
countries.note: Guyana's security picture has been transformed by its emergence as a major oil producer (2019 ExxonMobil strike — 700K+ bpd by 2025). The Venezuela-Guyana Essequibo territorial dispute, revived by Maduro's 2023 referendum, drove significant defence investment and a US-Brazil security partnership framework. The GDF is small but receiving rapid equipment and training upgrades. Civil-military relations are stable under Ali; oil-sector protection is the emerging military mission.
countries.watch: Venezuela's Essequibo territorial claim and oil-sector security are driving the first significant GDF expansion in decades. US and Brazil security partnerships are reshaping the strategic posture; monitor for any Venezuelan provocation post-Rodríguez transition.

countries.name: Haiti
countries.note: Haiti has had no elected government since President Moïse's assassination in July 2021. The unelected Transitional Presidential Council (April 2024) was dissolved in February 2026, leaving Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé with sole executive authority, with no president or sitting parliament. The Kenyan-led MSS mission gave way to a UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force in 2026. Its mandate was renewed through March 31, 2027, but it remains well short of its 5,500 target, and gangs control three of ten provinces. On October 6, 2026, the electoral council postponed indefinitely the elections planned for December 2026 and February 2027. The Haitian Army (FAd'H) has fewer than 2,000 troops and is largely ineffective; CMR is secondary to whether a functional state can be re-established.
countries.watch: CRITICAL. Elections planned for Dec 2026 and Feb 2027 were postponed indefinitely on Oct 6, 2026. The Gang Suppression Force mandate runs to Mar 31, 2027, but the force is far below its 5,500 target. Monitor GSF deployment, HNP reconstruction, PM Fils-Aimé's sole-executive legitimacy, and gang control of three of ten provinces.

election.note: Dec 13, 2026 first round and Feb 21, 2027 runoff postponed indefinitely on Oct 6, 2026.

countries.name: Jamaica
countries.branches: Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) · Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF)
countries.note: Jamaica has had the Caribbean's highest per-capita homicide rates among non-conflict states, though murders fell about 42% in 2025 to roughly 666, the lowest since 1994. Andrew Holness won a third term in September 2025. After Hurricane Melissa (October 2025), he moved the JDF out of the security ministry into a new Ministry of Defence in the Office of the Prime Minister (February 2026). Repeated Zones of Special Operations (ZOSOs) have normalized joint military-police domestic enforcement. Gang-state collusion in garrison communities is a long-standing structural issue.
countries.watch: Zone of Special Operations (ZOSO) normalization — monitor whether joint military-police operations become a permanent institutional feature and their effect on civil-military accountability and human rights norms.

missions.role: States of emergency (Zones of Special Operations)

countries.name: Suriname
countries.note: Suriname's CMR history is defined by Dési Bouterse, who led military coups in 1980 and 1990, served as president 2010–2020, and was convicted for the 1982 December Murders of 15 political opponents. He died a fugitive in December 2024. His party, the NDP, returned to power after the May 2025 elections, and Jennifer Geerlings-Simons became Suriname's first woman president in July 2025. The SNL retains institutional memory of direct rule. Suriname is a significant cocaine transit state, with documented links between trafficking interests and political actors, and offshore oil development is an emerging security mission.
countries.watch: Return of Bouterse's NDP to power under President Geerlings-Simons: watch December Murders accountability, SNL political neutrality, narco-transit penetration of the state, and the security demands of offshore oil.

countries.name: Trinidad and Tobago
countries.branches: Trinidad and Tobago Defence Force (TTDF) · TTPS
countries.note: Trinidad and Tobago has one of the hemisphere's highest murder rates relative to income, driven by gangs linked to Venezuelan trafficking networks. Kamla Persad-Bissessar's UNC government (since May 2025) split the national security portfolio into Defence and Homeland Security ministries. It also replaced the Chief of Defence Staff in October 2025, revoking one appointment the same day, and the police commissioner post has seen an acting appointment in September 2026. The TTDF's domestic role is expanding. T&T's proximity to post-Maduro Venezuela and its alignment with the US Caribbean counter-narcotics surge make it a key Caribbean monitoring case.
countries.watch: Persad-Bissessar's alignment with the US Caribbean counter-narcotics campaign and post-Maduro Venezuela spillover. Watch the restructured Defence and Homeland Security ministries, TTDF domestic deployments, and turnover in the defence and police leadership.

countries.name: Bolivia
countries.note: Bolivia experienced a contested coup/resignation crisis in November 2019, when Evo Morales left office after the military 'suggested' he resign, and a failed military uprising against Luis Arce in June 2024. Rodrigo Paz Pereira took office in November 2025, ending almost two decades of MAS rule. A wave of protests in mid-2026 produced a defence-ministry turnover; unofficial reports say the outgoing minister refused to sign a state-of-exception decree. A new high command under Gen. Víctor Hugo Balderrama was installed in June 2026. Whether the military is drawn into domestic order operations under the new government is the key CMR test.
countries.watch: Paz government amid mid-2026 protests: watch for state-of-exception decrees, military deployment for domestic order, the June 2026 high command's loyalty, and prosecutions linked to the June 2024 uprising.

countries.name: Colombia
countries.note: Colombia's civil–military environment is still shaped by the internal armed conflict. The right-wing De la Espriella government, in office since August 2026, has replaced the Petro-era 'Total Peace' approach with a hard-line security agenda. It is led by a retired-general defence minister and a new top command that includes reinstated officers. Institutional cohesion in the forces appears strong, and there are alignment risks around politicised appointments, the use of retired officers in command, and proposals on military justice through the JEP. U.S. cooperation continues to shape doctrine and equipment, and Colombia has also begun paying for Gripen aircraft.
countries.watch: Watch whether the reinstated-officer appointments, the push to defeat armed groups by force and the proposed new military-justice body create friction with courts, the JEP and human-rights oversight ahead of the October 2027 regional elections.

in_depth.subtitle: Peace Process · Armed Conflict · CMR
in_depth.brief: Colombia's civil-military relations are defined by a decades-long counter-insurgency legacy and the unfinished 2016 FARC peace process. The armed forces retain significant operational autonomy acquired during 50+ years of internal conflict, which structurally constrains Petro's Total Peace agenda. Three simultaneous negotiation tracks — FARC-EMC, ELN, and paramilitary successor groups — create competing military command authorities and fragmented territorial control.

countries.name: Ecuador
countries.note: Ecuador declared an 'internal armed conflict' in January 2024 following the televised storming of TC Televisión by armed criminal groups. President Noboa militarized internal security, granting the armed forces an expanded domestic mandate. This represents a significant formal shift in civil-military roles and is one of the most important CMR developments in the region in recent years.

Monitor whether US advisory embed becomes permanent, civilian judicial oversight of military operations, and ACHR proceedings over alleged torture and arbitrary detention.

countries.name: Peru
countries.note: Peru has experienced extreme executive instability; Keiko Fujimori, inaugurated July 28, 2026, is its ninth president in a decade. Congress removed Dina Boluarte in October 2025, after a tenure that relied heavily on the security forces to suppress protests following Castillo's failed December 2022 self-coup. Fujimori won the June 2026 runoff by fewer than 50,000 votes. Her election revives questions about the legacy of Alberto Fujimori's 1992 self-coup and military-intelligence nexus. Illegal mining and narco-trafficking in the VRAEM continue to drive military domestic deployment.
countries.watch: Keiko Fujimori's first months: watch the government's posture toward Boluarte-era protest killings cases, any amnesty or impunity legislation benefiting security forces, VRAEM and illegal-mining deployments, and whether a narrow mandate makes the presidency lean on the security forces.

last_election.note: Fujimori beat Roberto Sánchez by fewer than 50,000 votes.

countries.name: Venezuela
countries.branches: FANB: Army · Navy · Air Force · Guard · Militia
countries.note: Venezuela has been in a post-Maduro transition since Operation Absolute Resolve on January 3, 2026, when US special operations forces captured Nicolás Maduro in Caracas. Maduro was arraigned in New York on narco-terrorism charges on January 5, the day Acting President Delcy Rodríguez was sworn in. Rodríguez has since rebuilt the high command. On March 18 she replaced Vladimir Padrino López, defence minister since 2014, with former SEBIN and DGCIM chief Gen. Gustavo González López. She replaced the sanctioned CEOFANB commander Domingo Hernández Lárez in March, and that replacement in turn in July (Maj. Gen. Rubén Belzares Escobar). The constitutional six-month election window passed without a vote. At the UN in September 2026 Rodríguez promised elections but set no date. Venezuela remains the most critical CMR monitoring case in the hemisphere.
countries.watch: CRITICAL WATCH. Rodríguez has replaced Padrino López (Mar 2026) and rotated the CEOFANB twice. Monitor FANB cohesion under Defence Minister González López, DGCIM purges, colectivo demobilization, US conditions on the transition, and any concrete election timetable (none set as of Sep 2026). Maduro's New York prosecution is ongoing.

election.note: No date set. Rodríguez promised elections at the UN on Sep 23, 2026; the US says stabilization must come first.

in_depth.subtitle: FANB Structure · Authoritarian CMR · Succession
in_depth.brief: Venezuela represents the region's most advanced case of civil-military fusion. The Bolivarian Armed Forces (FANB) are structurally integrated into the economy, intelligence architecture, and political legitimation of the regime. The January 2026 Operation Absolute Resolve — the arrest of President Maduro by opposition forces and his transfer to US custody — creates an acute succession crisis with no precedent in SENTINEL's monitoring period.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.note: Brazil maintains the strongest formal civilian control architecture in South America. The 1988 constitution subordinates the armed forces to civilian authority, though institutional memory of the 1964–1985 military government remains. Ongoing debates center on the military's expanded role under Bolsonaro (2019–2022) and subsequent normalization efforts under Lula. The Escola Superior de Guerra and defense ministry reforms are key SSR indicators to watch.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.branches: Army · Navy · Air Force · GNA · PNA
countries.note: Argentina's military has been under firm civilian control since the restoration of democracy in 1983, shaped by accountability for Dirty War crimes (1976–1983). In December 2025 Milei named Lt. Gen. Carlos Presti, the former Army chief, as defence minister. Presti is the first military officer to hold the post since 1983, and a 2026 decree confirmed that active-duty officers may serve in it. Presti reshuffled the high command, appointing V. Adm. Marcelo Dalle Nogare to the Joint Staff and Gen. Oscar Zarich to the Army. Argentina's defence posture remains defensive and regionally cooperative, but the move erodes a core norm of the post-1983 civilian-control model.
countries.watch: Lt. Gen. Presti's tenure as the first military defence minister since 1983. Watch whether active-duty officers become normalized in civilian defence posts, any rollback of the domestic-security ban in the Internal Security Law, and Milei's 2027 re-election positioning.

countries.name: Chile
countries.note: Chile has the most professionalized armed forces in South America outside Brazil, and civilian control has been robust since the post-Pinochet transition. José Antonio Kast took office on March 11, 2026, the most right-wing president since the return to democracy. His defence minister, Fernando Barros, was Pinochet's spokesman during the 1998 London detention, and he named a retired army general as under-secretary for the armed forces. Gen. Pedro Varela, appointed by Boric, commands the Army for 2026–2030. Human-rights accountability for the dictatorship and for the 2019 uprising, northern-border militarization, and defence budget direction are the key early indicators.
countries.watch: Kast's government (since Mar 2026), with a former Pinochet spokesman as defence minister: track any moves on human-rights prosecutions and Punta Peuco, military deployment at the northern border and in critical infrastructure, and defence budget growth.

countries.name: Paraguay
countries.note: Paraguay's military maintains moderate institutional autonomy under a formally democratic system, but the Colorado Party's 75-year near-continuous rule has created a party-military patron-client network. The eastern border region (Triple Frontera) involves military and police forces in anti-narcotics and smuggling operations, with documented corruption concerns. Paraguay has no international conflict history in the modern era.
countries.watch: EPP guerrilla activity in the north and Triple Frontera OC operations are the primary drivers of military domestic deployment — and documented corruption.

countries.name: Uruguay
countries.note: Uruguay is consistently the strongest CMR case in Latin America on all civilian control metrics: lowest military spending, no internal deployment, robust accountability for dictatorship-era crimes, and professional civil-military relations. The small armed forces have a UN peacekeeping-heavy focus. Uruguay serves as a benchmark case for democratic civilian control in CMR comparative research.
countries.watch: Benchmark case for civilian control — watch for any changes to peacekeeping commitments under Orsi and whether the defense reform agenda continues.
